extracted.intended_audience: high-school newspaper editors / student journalists / make-up editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and composing (making up) high-school newspapers: page/column decisions, heading schedules, placement priorities, advertising rules, and type/illustration practices for first and inside pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary production decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before undertaking publication, the editors must decide how many pages the paper shall contain, how many columns there shall be on a page, and how wide each column shall be. They must work out a complete schedule of headings and select type suitable for headings and context. For the name at the top of the first page they must choose some sort of design, — either an electrotype or a hand-set title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These foundational choices (pages, columns, column width, heading schedule, type selection, and masthead design) should be made up front and determine subsequent make-up choices. A 'dummy' model page can be used later to test placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not copy daily newspapers' make-up
rubrics_metrics.description: The easiest way to solve these problems is to copy some good daily newspaper, but it is a way that never should be taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-school events are seldom startling enough for very large daily-style headlines; high-school papers don't compete for street sales, so they don't need striking make-up. Conservatism should govern make-up decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine pages and size by resources and news
rubrics_metrics.description: The number and size of the pages should be determined, of course, by financial resources and by the amount of really interesting news obtainable from week to week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid expanding layout beyond what budget and content justify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended column width
rubrics_metrics.description: The width of the columns should be that of the average column, twelve and one half or thirteen ems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this column measure as a standard for readable, newspaper-style measure in high-school papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headings size/style depend on paper size
rubrics_metrics.description: The number, size, and style of the headings should depend upon the size of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose heading types to fit the paper's column count and overall dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type-size recommendations for headings and context
rubrics_metrics.description: In a four- or five-column paper 18-point or 24-point type is large enough for the most important headings. In a six- or seven-column paper nothing larger than 30-point or 36-point type should be used. The best kind of type for context is the 8-point Roman used by most newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these type-size ceilings to keep proportionate and readable heading hierarchy; use 8-point Roman for body text.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-page title style
rubrics_metrics.description: Because fanciful designs are difficult to read and amateurish in appearance, plain black letters are best for the title at the top of the first page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek attractiveness and individuality of appearance rather than garishness and eccentricity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up editor uses schedule and proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When the stories and their headings have been set up, the make-up editor gives direction for their placement on the pages. In doing this work he has before him the news editor’s copy schedule and the galley proofs taken by the printer, and he checks off on the schedule and proofs the stories as they are placed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful copy scheduling and checking of galley proofs avoids the need for an elaborate dummy and prevents placement mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a 'dummy' model page is optional
rubrics_metrics.description: Some make-up editors find it necessary to use a 'dummy,' or model page, upon which have been pasted the stories and headings clipped from the galley proofs. If the copy schedule has been prepared carefully, however, the 'dummy' need not be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dummy pages can help visualize layout but are not required with a good copy schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority placement hierarchy for first-page stories
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. The most important position in a paper is the upper right-hand corner of the first page. The leading story — the story with the 'top heading' — should be placed here. 2. The second most important position is the upper left-hand corner of the first page. The story next in importance to the leading article should be placed here. 3. The parts of the middle columns just above the fold or middle of the page are next in order of importance. Then follow the right and left lower corners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this ordered list when assigning stories to positions so readers see the most important items first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress page toward balance when heavy headline used
rubrics_metrics.description: When a heavy headline is used for the leading story, the page should be 'dressed' toward the upper left-hand corner; that is, the lesser headings and illustrations should be centered on the left side of the page to 'balance' the 'top heading' and keep the reader’s attention on the first page until he has finished reading it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visual balancing (centering lesser elements) to counteract a dominant top headline and retain attention on page one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of cuts and cartoons
rubrics_metrics.description: If a cut or cartoon is used, it should be placed at the top of the page preferably, or at the bottom, and 'balanced' carefully with headlines so that it does not give the page a 'lopsided' appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations should augment, not unbalance, the page; when possible place at top or bottom and coordinate with headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance headlines but avoid geometric plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: Care should be taken to balance the headlines; that is, to make the appearance of the page symmetrical, but geometric plotting should be avoided. Many offenses are committed in the name of balance. A page should not be made to look like a dress-goods pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for aesthetic balance without forced, mechanical symmetry that looks patterned or artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid adjacent-column headline grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines in adjoining columns should not be placed together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing neighboring-column headlines flush with each other makes them difficult to read and weakens their appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-page content: only important news
rubrics_metrics.description: Only important news stories should be placed on the first page. Editorials, jokes, feature stories, and brevities should be put inside. The first page of a newspaper is like a show window; it should contain only the best and latest news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve page one for the most newsworthy items to present a strong 'show window' impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use many stories on first page but avoid continuations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is good to use as many stories as possible on the first page, for numerous headlines give the paper a lively appearance, and short stories with small headings are useful in making up. It is a bad practice, however, to put small parts of stories on the first page and then continue them on an inside page. One of the first purposes of make-up is to keep the reader’s attention on a page until he has looked at all the stories it contains. If he turns the page to read the continuation of a story, the probability is that he will not turn back to the first page. Continuations are annoying to the reader and are often the cause of ridiculous blunders on the part of the printer. If a story is too long to be printed on the first page, it may be continued on another page. Otherwise it should be kept on the first page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer complete short items on page one; only continue longer stories when unavoidable and plan continuations carefully to avoid reader annoyance and printing errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department-page system: limited use
rubrics_metrics.description: The department system of handling material is over-worked frequently in high school papers. It is well to designate one page — preferably the second, in a four-page paper — as the editorial page, to set aside one page for sports, and to give club news the leading position on another. But to carry the department idea further is inadvisable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a modest department structure (editorial, sports, club pages) but avoid rigidly compartmentalizing every page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisements placement rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements should never be printed on the first page. Few or none should be placed on the editorial page. The make-up editor should arrange the advertisements tastefully and should try to place as many of them as possible next to reading matter. Some advertisers will purchase space only upon condition that their advertisements be given certain positions. The make-up editor must place these 'preferred space' advertisements first and use his best judgment in arranging the rest. So far as possible, the advertising staff should avoid the sale of 'preferred space.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep ads off page one; minimize ads on editorial page; place preferred-space ads as required but otherwise place ads adjacent to reading matter and avoid selling fixed preferred positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pyramid ad layout on ad pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements should be 'pyramided' on the right side of the page, with the peak of the pyramid at the top. On pages carrying advertisements, therefore, the leading story should be placed at the upper left-hand corner. It is exceedingly bad form to print advertisements in both outside columns and put the reading matter in the center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use right-side pyramiding of ads and avoid flanking pages with ads in both outer columns while centralizing content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage number of display headings
rubrics_metrics.description: When too many display headings have been written, the make-up editor should ask the news editor to 'lower' some of them. . A paper with too many large headings looks as if its face needed washing. When there are not enough 'top heads' to make up the paper, the news editor may be asked to 'raise' some of the smaller headings. It should be remembered, however, that headlines are written to fit stories, not to balance make-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaborate with news editor to adjust heading prominence, but do not let make-up dictate story content or headline truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial page masthead and content order
rubrics_metrics.description: At the upper left-hand corner of the editorial page should be a two-column 'mast head,' carrying the name of the paper, statistics of publication, and names of the staff members. Below this should be placed the editorials, set either in single-column or in double-column measure. Other matter under special headings on the page may be: communications to the editor; humor; literary contributions, such as stories, essays, and poems; exchanges; alumni news; school brevities; and special features. Straight news stories should seldom be printed on the editorial page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this conventional editorial-page structure to separate opinion and feature material from straight news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sport-page make-up rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The sport page is made up much like the first page, except that the leading sport article is placed at the upper left corner instead of the upper right. A banner line across the top of the page may be used, if desired, to announce the principal event of the week. Cuts liven the appearance of the page but are too expensive to be used often unless they can be borrowed. It is inadvisable to use an electrotype with drawings at the top of the sport page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sport pages similarly to front pages but place the lead at upper left; be sparing with cuts and avoid expensive electrotype drawings at the top.

rubrics_metrics.name: Club-news and back-page headings
rubrics_metrics.description: The club news, under a two-column headline, makes a good leader for the back page. It is good, though not necessary, to have a two-column heading to lead every page of a seven-column paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two-column club-news leads on the back page and consider two-column leads to balance seven-column papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedule A heading system (five-column paper)
rubrics_metrics.description: The six kinds of headings included in Schedule A are sufficient for the make-up of a five-column paper. For stories of extraordinary importance the top bank of the No. 1 heading may be made two columns wide to form a 2-over-1 head (z.e. 2-column top bank over 1-column lower banks). The headings are numbered according to the size of type in the top bank, the largest being designated No. 1, the next largest No. 2, etc. The minimum and maximum numbers of units permissible in each line of type are given on each heading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Schedule A as a standard heading set for five-column papers; understand the meaning of notations like 2-over-1 for special wide top banks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting units for heading lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: In counting units begin with the first letter in the line and count all letters and spaces except the space between the last letter and the rule. Count the letters m and w one and one-half units each and the letter 7 one-half unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this unit-counting method to ensure headings fit prescribed unit ranges for each heading class. (Preserve exact counting rules as given.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedule B heading system (seven-column paper) and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The twelve kinds of headings included in Schedule B are sufficient for the make-up of all pages of a seven-column paper. The single-column headings are numbered according to the sizes of type in their top banks, the largest being designated as No. 1, the second largest as No. 2, etc. The two-column headings are numbered 2-over-1 and 2-over-4. Headings No. 2-over-4, 4, and 5 are not used on page one. Headings No. 2-over-1, 1, 2, and 3 are used only on page one. Headings No. 6, 7, 9, and 10 are used on both page one and the inside pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Schedule B's mapping of heading numbers to page use when composing seven-column papers; reserve certain heading types for page one only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedule C heading system (six- or seven-column paper) and feature headings
rubrics_metrics.description: The ten kinds of headings included in Schedule C are sufficient for the make-up of a six-column or seven-column paper. The regular news headings are numbered according to the sizes of type in their top banks, the largest heading being designated as No. 1, the next largest as No. 2, etc. The feature-story headings are lettered, the smallest being designated as A, the next larger as B, and the largest as C. No subhead is shown in the schedule. An 8-point capital and lower-case subhead, 25 to 31 units in length, is used. Brevities are given no headings, but the first lines are set in bold-face type. The feature headings are used on all pages and are useful in balancing the make-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Schedule C when appropriate; apply lettered feature headings (A,B,C), and set subheads and brevities per the described conventions to help balance pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations and heading schedules usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The following illustrations give head schedules suitable for five-, six-, and seven-column papers and show some of the page make-ups that may be formed with them. Note: Illustrations show headings reduced to 50 per cent of their actual size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the supplied plate examples (Schedules A,B,C and plates) to visualize recommended heading sizes and page make-ups; remember illustrations in the book may be reduced.
